summary.one_line: India's largest institutional on-campus student-housing operator is a real business with a scale lead, but this Rs 2,100 crore all-fresh issue mostly pays for promoter-group school assets (Rs 1,100 crore) and debt repayment (Rs 750 crore). Its FY26 profit jump rests on a one-off gain, it carries heavy leverage, and occupancy is falling. For a retail applicant the issue looks more like the promoter cashing out than new capital for the business.
bull_points: Clear scale leader in professionally managed student accommodation (PMSA): 78,542 beds as of June 15, 2026, about 2.1x the second-largest PMSA operator and 6.2x the third (S3, S13). CBRE also calls it the largest owner-operator of beds in the segment (S9).

The owned model rests on long HEI agreements (30-60 years in the ownership model) with minimum-occupancy guarantees, whose weighted average is 87.55% (S9, S2). The Dubai school buildings are on triple-net leases with 10-30 year lock-ins and 3-5% annual escalations (S2).
Revenue from operations rose from Rs 347.00 crore (FY24) to Rs 568.63 crore (FY26), and normalised EBITDA margin widened from 63.5% to 72.9% (S6, S2).
All of the issue is fresh shares, with no offer for sale. The promoter keeps 65.58% after the issue (S1, S3).

Structural demand: CBRE estimates a gap of about 0.21 million beds in the target addressable market, and projects PMSA annual revenue potential growing from US$2.53 bn (AY2024-25) to US$3.78 bn (AY2027-28), a 14% CAGR (S9).
bear_points: Rs 1,100 crore (52.38%) of the proceeds buys 16 K-12 entities and campuses from fellow subsidiaries of the Hillhouse-controlled promoters. In Value Research's words, you are 'funding the promoter's exit from assets held in related entities' (S14, S2, S10).
The largest target, PE Bowenpally (enterprise value Rs 593.30 crore), faces a pending Benami Property notice from the Income Tax Department and a Telangana High Court lake-buffer case (S10, S11).
Borrowings rose from Rs 984.71 crore (FY24) to Rs 4,120.53 crore (FY26), debt-to-equity is about 4.98x, and 66.61% of borrowings carry floating rates (S1, S6, S5).
FY26 PAT of Rs 173.76 crore includes an exceptional gain of Rs 104.9 crore from a hostel sale. Adjusted PAT is about Rs 68.8 crore, and ROCE fell to 6.4% from 9.9% (S2).
Owned-bed occupancy fell to 89.37% in AY2025-26 from 99.47% the year before and 99.92% in AY2023-24 (S6, S4).
Parent Genius Assetco has pledged 100% of the promoter holding companies' shares to secure offshore financing (S2).
watch_points: Whether the Benami and lake-buffer proceedings at PE Bowenpally are resolved before the Rs 1,100 crore is paid out (S11).
Owned-bed occupancy in AY2026-27, including re-letting of the vacated 1,162-bed Woodstock hostel in Bengaluru (S2).
Delivery on the director's statement that debt-to-EBITDA can fall to about 4x by March 2027 (S15).
Whether the promoter pledge that was released before the IPO is re-created after listing (S2).
Final subscription numbers by category; day-1 data was not yet meaningful when this was written (S23).

reasoning: Little of the money goes into the business. Rs 1,100 crore goes to promoter-affiliated sellers for K-12 assets and Rs 750 crore repays borrowings, much of it at subsidiaries that bought recent acquisitions. Only the implied balance of up to about Rs 250 crore (before issue expenses) is left for inorganic growth and general purposes (S14, S2).

The related-party acquisition carries unresolved legal risk. The biggest asset being bought, PE Bowenpally, has a live Benami notice and a pending High Court lake-buffer case. Aggregate equity value of Rs 1,115.71 crore is being paid on enterprise values set by a promoter-group transaction (S10, S11).

Earnings quality is weaker than the headline. Excluding a Rs 104.9 crore exceptional gain, FY26 PAT was about Rs 68.8 crore. ROCE fell to 6.4% while borrowings roughly quadrupled in two years to Rs 4,120.53 crore (S2, S1).

The moat is real but narrower than the pitch. Scale leadership and long HEI contracts are genuine advantages. Against that, three HEIs still make up 61.46% of revenue (O.P. Jindal alone about 36%), and owned-bed occupancy has dropped about 10 points in a year (S4, S6).

Governance needs watching. The promoter chain is fully pledged to offshore lenders, the Dubai schools were bought under common control for Rs 1,092.495 crore months before the IPO, and KMP attrition was 40% (S2, S12, S5).

For a retail applicant, the better course is to skip the IPO and revisit after listing, once there are 2-3 quarters of disclosed occupancy, the post-acquisition leverage and the legal outcome at Bowenpally. That makes this 'avoid' for the issue itself, not a permanent rejection of the business (S15, S11).

subsections.title: What the company does and how it earns money

blocks.text: Elevate Campuses owns, operates and manages on-campus student accommodation for higher education institutions (HEIs), and also owns K-12 school real estate. It operates under the 'Good Host Spaces' and 'ScholarZ' brands (S3, S7). It was incorporated in 2005 as Woodstock Ambience Private Limited, began student-accommodation operations in FY2018, and took the Elevate Campuses name in September 2025 (S8).

Revenue comes in two main forms. In the owned ('PropCo + OpCo') model, the company buys or takes long leases on hostel blocks from a university, runs them, and keeps 100% of the student fees. HEI agreements in this model run 30-60 years and usually include minimum-occupancy guarantees and fee escalations (S9, S13). In the managed ('ManCo') model, the HEI keeps the asset and the revenue, and the operator earns a management fee that CBRE puts at 10-15% of gross revenue (S9, S13). The owned portfolio dominates: 65.74% of FY26 operating revenue came from student accommodation in the Owned Portfolio (S7).

The K-12 business is a landlord business, not a school-operating business. The two Dubai schools, Hartland International School and North London Collegiate School, are leased on triple-net terms with 10-30 year lock-ins and 3-5% annual rent escalations (S2). Hartland is run by Meraki Education under a long-term lease, sits on nine acres of freehold land in Mohammed Bin Rashid City, and serves over 2,000 students (S17).

The weighted-average minimum occupancy guaranteed by HEIs is 87.55% (S2). Because of this contractual floor, owned-bed revenue behaves more like a lease annuity than hotel-style income, but the floor is below the 99%+ occupancy the company used to earn.

blocks.caption: Portfolio scale at different dates (as disclosed)

blocks.text: Operationally this is closer to hospitality than real estate. The company runs 62 retail outlets across its portfolio (S7), serves more than 50,000 meals a day and handles over 1,562 service requests a day (S5). It had 460 full-time employees as of March 31, 2026 (S6). The CEO describes it as 'a very operations-intensive business, not just real estate', covering cafeterias, laundry and gyms (S15). Revenue is geographically concentrated: 70.13% comes from northern and southern India (S7).

Most growth in the last 18 months came from acquisitions. It bought Zolo's on-campus hostel business (Rs 124.19 crore, April 2025) and Data Ram Sons Private Limited (Rs 435.62 crore, December 2025). It also bought hostel assets from Manav Rachna (reported as 'Mavan Rachna') Universities (Rs 103.52 crore, February 2026) and an SH-11 hostel block (Rs 166.196 crore, March 2026). The Dubai schools came through Elevate UAE Assetco (Rs 1,092.495 crore, September 2025, from a common-control entity) (S12).

About 74% of operated beds (58,174 of 78,542) are not owned (S13). These carry lower fees and less contractual protection than owned beds, so the headline bed count overstates the share of annuity-like income.

The customers are effectively the partner universities, even though students pay the fees. Named partners include Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal University Jaipur, O.P. Jindal Global University and Shoolini University, plus an IIT Madras hostel development (S7, S18). In K-12, Meraki Education operates Hartland in Dubai (S17).

Concentration is high but falling. The top three HEIs contributed about 89% of revenue in FY25 and 61.46% in FY26 (S2, S4). O.P. Jindal Global University alone accounted for about 36% of FY26 revenue (S4). Value Research notes that the FY26 fall in the top-3 share came mainly from adding Dubai school revenue, not from diversifying across universities (S2).

items: Any dispute, regulatory action or enrolment drop at O.P. Jindal would hit roughly a third of revenue (S4).
The CBRE industry report itself names HEI mismanagement or reputational damage, which PMSA operators cannot control, as a key sector risk (S9).
One Bengaluru hostel (Woodstock, 1,162 beds) went vacant after its lease was terminated in September 2025, which shows single-asset risk (S2).

blocks.text: The industry data comes from a CBRE South Asia report commissioned by the company, dated September 26, 2025 (S9). CBRE projects higher-education enrolment rising from 49.30 million (AY2024-25E) to 56.18 million (AY2027-28F). Its target addressable market (TAM) is private universities and colleges above hostel-size thresholds plus Institutes of National Importance, with enrolment projected to grow from 3.55 million to 4.56 million over the same period (S9).

CBRE puts the current demand-supply gap within the TAM at about 0.21 million beds, and the gap across all higher education at 1.67 million beds (S9). It sizes the management-model opportunity at 3.03 million beds in AY2024-25, growing at an 8% CAGR to 3.80 million by AY2027-28 (S9). As of June 2025 there were about 1.5-1.6 lakh operational PMSA beds in India (S9).

These are commissioned figures, and CBRE states it relied on client-supplied data about the company without testing it (S9). The market is growing, but a 14% revenue-potential CAGR describes the market, not a guaranteed growth rate for Elevate.

CBRE names Stanza Living, Your Space, Isthara, Curated Living, Hello World, Tribe Living, Colive, Hive Hostels and Olive Living as active operators (S9). Only five operators have more than 5,000 PMSA beds. As of August 2025, CBRE's (anonymised) ranking put the company first with 66,272 beds, followed by operators with 38,000-43,000, 11,000-13,000, 8,000-10,000 and 7,000-9,000 beds (S9). Most rivals are asset-light (OpCo/lease models) backed by venture or growth capital, for example General Atlantic in Your Space and Peak XV/Accel in Stanza Living (S9).

blocks.caption: Largest PMSA operators, CBRE as of Aug 2025 (S9)
rows: Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Pune

blocks.text: Elevate also faces the unorganised sector. PGs charge less and often avoid the 18% GST that organised operators pay on leased residential property, which is a real threat in price-sensitive off-campus markets (S9). Beds are also competing with each HEI's option to keep running its own hostels.

There is a moat, but a moderate one built on capital and relationships, not technology or regulation. CBRE says Elevate is the largest owner-operator in PMSA, and that the ownership model is practised only by a few operators because it is capital-intensive (S9). HEIs prefer established, institutionally backed operators, and access to trust-owned university land is hard for newcomers (S9). The company's scale lead widened from about 1.7x the next operator (August 2025) to about 2.1x (June 2026) (S9, S3).

items: Real advantages: long HEI contracts with occupancy floors, the capital to buy hostel blocks outright, and the largest bed base (S9, S2).
Limits: no regulatory licence or technology barrier. Deep-pocketed investors (General Atlantic, Warburg Pincus earlier) are funding rivals (S9).
Contract terms protect each individual campus, but they do not stop competitors from winning the next university mandate.
Market-share claims should be read with care. One secondary summary puts ECL at 44-46% of about 1.7-1.8 lakh PMSA beds, but that includes managed beds the company does not own (S13).

blocks.text: Verdict on the moat: genuine scale and contract advantages in owned on-campus housing, which explain the high normalised EBITDA margins. It is not an import-substitution or regulatory moat.

Revenue grew 6.6% in FY25 and 53.8% in FY26 (S4, S6). The FY26 jump mainly reflects acquisitions: the Dubai schools, Zolo's on-campus business, Data Ram Sons and additional hostel blocks (S12). Same-portfolio growth was modest, and FY25 growth of about 6.6% is the cleaner guide to the base business's organic pace.

The reported FY26 EBITDA margin of about 90% and the 3.5x PAT jump are distorted by a Rs 104.9 crore exceptional gain from selling a hostel (S2, S6). On an underlying basis, PAT was roughly Rs 68.8 crore (S2). Treat 'profit tripled' headlines as misleading.

Borrowings more than tripled in FY26 as the company paid for acquisitions with debt. Debt-to-equity is about 4.98x (S6, S7); another summary puts it at 5.04x (S5). Value Research estimates net debt-to-EBITDA at 6.23x when the exceptional gain is excluded (S2). 66.61% of borrowings are floating-rate, so interest rates directly affect profit (S5). Some growth was also funded with Rs 1,050 crore of CCDs issued to a shareholder group company, which are to convert into equity (S12).

Management gives a different debt figure. Director Mukesh Tiwari has put current debt at about Rs 3,400 crore, falling to about Rs 2,600-2,700 crore after the Rs 750 crore repayment (S15). This probably reflects a net or post-conversion measure, but the sources we accessed do not reconcile it with the restated Rs 4,120.53 crore.

Gap: we could not access the restated cash-flow statement (operating cash flow vs PAT) or working-capital detail, because the RHP/DRHP PDFs could not be fetched. The cash-flow/profit match therefore could not be checked.

subsections.title: Does the trend support the growth story?

blocks.text: Partly. Normalised EBITDA margins have genuinely widened, from 63.5% to 72.9% (S2), which fits a high-fixed-cost asset base filling up and adding higher-yield school leases. But return on capital is falling (ROCE 9.9% to 6.4%) because acquisitions were paid for at prices their current earnings do not yet support, and financed with debt (S2).

items: Management's 'latest year revenue' figure of about Rs 807 crore, split roughly 55% student accommodation and 45% K-12 by EBITDA, appears to be pro forma including the K-12 targets. It is not the restated Rs 568.63 crore (S15, S5).
Occupancy fell by about 10 points in one year, from 99.47% to 89.37% (S6). Guaranteed floors limit the revenue damage, but the trend undercuts the 'full hostels' story.
The CEO's claim of 'margins of around 19-20%' could not be reconciled with any restated metric in the sources we accessed (S15).

blocks.text: The issue shrank between the DRHP and the RHP. The DRHP filed with SEBI (October 2025) was reported at Rs 2,550 crore (S8, S25), and one report cites a Rs 1,850 crore fresh-issue figure (S5). The final RHP issue is Rs 2,100 crore (S1).

Retail gets only 10% of the book because QIBs get at least 75% (S1). One aggregator reported a 50/15/35 split (S19), but most sources and the anchor size (Rs 945 crore, 60% of a Rs 1,575 crore QIB book) are consistent with 75/15/10 (S3, S20).

blocks.text: The 16 K-12 targets include JIRS (Kanakapura), St. Andrews Suchitra and Keesara (Hyderabad), St. Michael's Alwal and St. Michael's Mariah International, Shri Ram Universal School (Chennai), JPS campuses (Andhra Pradesh), Billabong High International (Pune), SET (Bengaluru), and an IFM College hostel (Bengaluru) (S10). Their aggregate enterprise value is Rs 1,824.62 crore. The largest are PE Bowenpally (Rs 593.30 crore) and PE Chennai (Rs 188.57 crore) (S10).

The fact that there is no OFS is formally positive: every rupee goes to the company. In economic terms, though, more than half flows straight to entities indirectly owned by the same Hillhouse funds that control the promoters (S10). Value Research calls the IPO 'primarily a monetisation event for the promoter, not a capital-raising for the business' (S2).

The debt being repaid includes loans at subsidiaries that hold the Dubai schools (Souk HIS/NLCS UAE) and Data Ram Sons (S14). These are debts taken on to buy assets, some from a common-control entity, only months before the IPO (S12).

The promoters are Genius Bidco Holdings Pte. Ltd. and Genius Rajkot Investment Holdings Pte. Ltd., Singapore entities ultimately owned by funds of Hillhouse Investment (S1, S4, S10). Good Host Spaces was founded in 2017, with Goldman Sachs owning about 70% and Warburg Pincus investing from 2021. In October 2023 both sold 100% to Alta Capital for about US$320 million (about Rs 2,700 crore), then India's largest student-housing deal, when the company had about 25,000 beds (S18). Rava Partners, described as 'the real assets arm of Hillhouse Investment', launched Elevate in 2023 with Alta Capital as its Indian operating partner (S17).

The promoter is a financial sponsor, not a founder-operator. It has held the business for about three years, has more than tripled the bed base largely through acquisitions, and is now selling promoter-group school assets into the listed company. Its long-run commitment will show in whether it keeps its 65.58% stake after lock-in expires (S1).

Parent Genius Assetco Holdings has pledged 100% of the shares of both promoter entities to secure offshore financing. A direct pledge on 22.1 million Elevate shares held by Genius Bidco was released just before the IPO but may be re-created after listing (S2). If the parent defaults elsewhere, control could change hands.

items: Chairman: A. N. Roy, Independent Director (S6).
CEO: Narasimha Jayakumar, who fronted the IPO roadshow comments on margins and operating intensity (S15, S16).
CFO and Whole-Time Director: Vinod Raja Rao (S6).

Other board members: Siddharth Gupta, Joseph Raymond Gagnon, Mukesh Tiwari, Rashmi Joshi (S6). A Siddhartha Gupta, formerly Managing Director of Blackstone India, led Alta Capital's 2023 purchase (S18). This appears to be the same sponsor-side person, but we could not confirm it from the RHP.
Director Mukesh Tiwari gave the post-IPO leverage guidance (S15).

blocks.text: Management depth is a concern. Employee attrition was 56.43% and key-managerial-personnel attrition was 40% (S5). In a business the CEO himself calls operations-intensive (S15), that turnover matters. We could not verify detailed biographies or tenures of the KMPs from the primary filing.

This RPT section is not routine. It is at the centre of the deal. (1) In September 2025 the company bought Elevate UAE Assetco (the Dubai schools) for Rs 1,092.495 crore from Elevate Mena Master Holdings, a common-control entity, and accounted for it by pooling of interests (S12). (2) Rs 1,100 crore of IPO money will buy 16 K-12 assets from fellow subsidiaries of the promoters (S10). (3) Rs 1,050 crore of CCDs were issued to a shareholder group company for conversion into equity (S12).

blocks.caption: Litigation and tax exposure disclosed (S11)
rows: Benami Prohibition Unit notice under s.19, Benami Act (June 14, 2024)
Lake-buffer construction case, Telangana High Court (notice Aug 2, 2023)
1 case, Rs 9.683 crore (indirect tax; appeal filed Mar 24, 2026)

blocks.text: We found no report of SEBI or exchange enforcement against the company itself. The governance issue is structural: the controlling shareholder sits on both sides of the largest use of proceeds, and the target assets carry legal clouds (S10, S11).

items: Related-party pricing: Rs 1,100 crore is paid to promoter affiliates for assets whose enterprise values (Rs 1,824.62 crore aggregate) were set within the group (S10).
Legal title and regulatory cloud on the largest target: the Benami notice and lake-buffer High Court case at PE Bowenpally (EV Rs 593.30 crore) (S11).
Leverage and rates: borrowings of Rs 4,120.53 crore, D/E about 4.98x, and 66.61% floating-rate exposure (S1, S6, S5).
HEI concentration: top 3 at 61.46% of FY26 revenue and O.P. Jindal at about 36% (S4).
Occupancy slippage: owned beds at 89.37% in AY2025-26 vs 99.47% a year earlier; the 1,162-bed Woodstock hostel vacated (S6, S2).
Promoter pledge: 100% of promoter entities pledged by the parent to offshore lenders (S2).
Execution and integration: several greenfield projects under construction need regulatory approvals, and 16 school assets are being absorbed at once (S22, S10).
People: 56.43% employee attrition and 40% KMP attrition (S5).

blocks.text: Of these, the first two directly decide whether the IPO money creates value. Leverage and concentration decide how much earnings volatility a shareholder is exposed to.

CBRE highlights several sector risks: operators depend on HEI governance and reputation, which they cannot control; tax treatment is unclear, with 18% GST on leased residential property unless exemption thresholds apply; and unorganised PGs compete on price (S9). Long HEI contracts also cut both ways. CBRE notes HEIs themselves face risk if service quality slips over a multi-decade contract (S9), so the company's reputation for service is its licence to win renewals.
The K-12 landlord model shifts school-operating risk to operators like Meraki, but rent depends on those operators' health and on enrolment at each school (S17, S2).

items: Leverage: debt-to-EBITDA to fall 'from around 6-7 times to roughly five times' after the Rs 750 crore repayment, with potential to reach '4 times by March 2027' (director Mukesh Tiwari) (S15).
Debt: current debt put at about Rs 3,400 crore, expected at Rs 2,600-2,700 crore after the IPO (S15).
Margins: the CEO says margins have expanded for three consecutive years, 'We would like to maintain the same trajectory going forward' (S15).
Liquidity and appetite: 'We have Rs 500 crores at any time and the tailwinds in Indian education opportunity are enormous' (CEO) (S16).
Financing model: lenders historically finance about 7-8x EBITDA at asset level, on 15-20 year tenures (S15).

blocks.text: Management has not published concrete bed-addition targets, occupancy guidance or revenue guidance in any source we accessed. The stated plan is to complete the K-12 acquisitions, cut leverage, and keep acquiring (S14, S15). The emphasis on lender capacity of '7-8 times EBITDA' suggests the company will keep financing growth with debt after the IPO.

The post-IPO company will be a hybrid: a student-housing operator plus a K-12 landlord, with K-12 contributing about 45% of EBITDA on management's pro forma framing (S15). Growth will come mainly from buying assets, not from filling existing beds. That makes capital allocation discipline, and the prices paid to related parties, the main driver of shareholder returns.
Management's leverage path depends on EBITDA growing as projected. With owned occupancy already down about 10 points (S6), the 4x target by March 2027 is an aspiration, not a commitment.

subsections.title: Anchor book, day-1 status and grey market

blocks.text: Before the issue opened, the company raised Rs 945 crore from anchor investors (S21). Reports say this came from about 20 domestic and international investors, including SBI Mutual Fund and Mirae Asset, and filled 60% of the institutional portion (S20). Up to 60% of the QIB portion was eligible for anchors, with one-third of that reserved for domestic mutual funds (S14). The specific lock-in dates were not published in the sources we accessed; SEBI rules impose a lock-in on anchor allocations.

This report was written on September 23, 2026, the day the issue opened. Trackers checked that day still showed subscription at 0x across categories, meaning no meaningful day-1 data was available yet (S23). No QIB, NII or retail multiple should be inferred until the exchanges publish bid data at the close of day 1 and later days.
GMP is unofficial, unregulated and volatile. A premium of Rs 5-16 on a Rs 362 upper band is small (about 1-4%) and is not an investment signal. It played no part in our verdict.

method: Searched for the DRHP/RHP and located both: the DRHP on SEBI's filing page and NSE archives, and the RHP (dated Sept 17, 2026) mirrored on chittorgarh.net. Neither PDF could be read directly. The NSE DRHP fetch timed out, the RHP exceeded the fetch size limit, and downloading via shell was not permitted. RHP-level facts (objects, K-12 targets and enterprise values, litigation, acquisitions, pledge, concentration, occupancy, restated financials) were therefore cross-verified across several secondary sources that quote the RHP: Chittorgarh, Value Research, Sushil Finance, Business Today, IndiaIPO, Paytm Money, ScanX and several Multibagg RHP digests. One primary document was read directly: the CBRE industry report (dated Sept 26, 2025) hosted on the company's website, used for all market-size and competitor data. Discrepancies are flagged in the text: revenue from operations vs total income; reported vs normalised EBITDA (FY26 includes a Rs 104.9 crore exceptional gain); D/E of 4.98x vs 5.04x; allocation reported as 75/15/10 by most sources but 50/15/35 by one; management's Rs 3,400 crore debt and Rs 807 crore revenue figures vs restated Rs 4,120.53 crore and Rs 568.63 crore. Material gaps: the restated cash-flow statement (operating cash flow vs PAT) and working-capital detail; the exact split of the residual proceeds between inorganic growth, GCP and issue expenses; full KMP biographies; the anchor lock-in dates and full anchor list. Day-1 subscription data was not yet meaningful at the time of writing. Valuation metrics volunteered by sources (P/E, P/B, market cap) were deliberately excluded. GMP is reported only as unofficial and was not used in the verdict. Three items (S20, S23, S25) come from search-result snippets because the pages returned 403 when opened.
